claims.text: A nanoscale Ni interlayer on W particles will promote in-situ reactive bonding during spark-plasma sintering and subsequent Cu infiltration.
The Ni interlayer will eliminate interfacial voids and defects in the W-Cu composite.
Interfacial voids and defects impair thermal transport and mechanical durability under irradiation.
A uniform nanoscale Ni coating can be applied to W particles by electroless plating before spark-plasma sintering and Cu infiltration.
The proposed spark-plasma sintering regime is approximately 1200-1400 °C under vacuum.
The proposed Cu infiltration regime is approximately 1080-1100 °C under an inert atmosphere.
The Ni interlayer lowers the interfacial energy between W and Cu.
Lower interfacial energy and reactive diffusion bonding produce near-perfect W-Cu interfacial contact.
The Ni coating enhances Cu wettability at the W-Cu interface.
The Ni coating fosters chemical interaction at the W-Cu interface during consolidation.
Enhanced wettability and interfacial chemical interaction reduce void formation and create more continuous interfacial regions.
Reducing interfacial voids minimizes phase separation and void-induced thermal-transport barriers.
The Ni-mediated interface preserves or enhances mechanical durability under irradiation.
Relative to identically processed material without an interlayer, Ni-coated W-Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to the uncoated baseline, Ni-coated W-Cu composites will have improved mechanical robustness during thermal cycling and irradiation.
The intervention is expected to remain effective under thermal cycling up to approximately 600 °C with simulated irradiation.
Analogous improvements have been observed for vapor-coated powders in similar systems.
Intermetallic-phase formation at the Ni-containing interface could reduce the thermal conduction of Cu.
